summary:
We developed Zenit, an educational narrative space mission simulator built with Vue 3, TypeScript, and a Python/FastAPI simulation engine. Acting as mission director across 10 interactive stages, from negotiating funding in visual-novel hearings and assembling spacecraft and crew in a hangar, to resolving transit anomalies and operating science and communications consoles inside a 2D pixel-art spacecraft deck players plan, launch, and evaluate a crewed expedition to Low Earth Orbit or Lunar Orbit.

Zenit addresses the challenge by turning interconnected aerospace trade-offs into playable, transparent consequences. Real engineering relationships—the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, NASA-referenced engine specific impulses and MMRTG power output, eclipse battery autonomy, life-support reserves, and bitrate-to-gigabyte transmission limits—directly link mass, delta-v, energy, budget (Créditos Zenit), and crew morale without artificial warnings hiding mistakes.

This matters because students and newcomers experience firsthand how engineering margins, financial pressure, and human factors determine mission success, building practical systems-thinking skills through a multi-ending evaluation.
details:
We built Zenit, a 10-stage narrative space mission game designed to give young students a friendly, approachable way to get familiar with how spaceflight works.

Stepping into the role of Captain Dog, players negotiate funding in front of a 3-cat review board, assemble spacecraft components and hire crew in a hangar, handle anomalies during transit, and walk around a 2D pixel-art ship to collect and send scientific data back to Earth before facing a multi-ending final debrief.

Instead of giving away hints or preselected answers, we wanted players to genuinely think through every choice and watch cause and effect happen live: heavier instruments lower delta-v through the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, smaller antennas bottleneck data transmission, and exceeding the launcher mass limit causes launch failure.

When designing the balance, our team carefully weighed realism against accessibility, anchoring physics in real NASA references like Apollo 8 lunar delta-v, RL10 and OMS-E propulsion specific impulses, and MMRTG power, while intentionally scaling total ship mass to 1,300 kg and using a fictional currency called Créditos Zenit so students focus on trade-offs rather than intimidating billion-dollar budgets.

We developed the game using Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, HTML5 Canvas, and Web Audio on the frontend, paired with a modular Python and FastAPI simulation engine, an offline browser fallback, and automated testing with Pytest, Vitest, and Playwright.
